newsitem.title: SYRIA: Big share for investment in Syria's 97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Big share for investment in Syria's 97 budget.

text.p: Syria's parliament on Sunday began discussing a 1997 draft budget that allocates the largest share to investment ever planned, officials said on Sunday.

They said the draft, presented by Finance Minister Khaled Mahayni on Saturday, set expenditure at 211.125 billion Syrian pounds ($4.85 billion) of which 108.7 billion ($2.5 billion) would go for investment and the rest current expenditure.
Revenues were projected at 211.125 pounds, but included local and foreign loans to cover the deficit in the budget for year beginning January 1, 1997, officials said.
They did not give a figure for the expected deficit and the finance minister's report, obtained by Reuters on Sunday, did not mention it. Final figures for a year are approved over four years later.

Syrian ministries have been spending on allocations based on the 1996 budget that set spending at 188.05 billion pounds. The new budget must be approved by parliament and issued by President Hafez al-Assad.

Economic sources said the real increase in the 1997 budget over last year was only 12.064 billion pounds, while the other 11.011 billion pounds was caused by changing the exchange rate from 23 pounds to 35 pounds to a U.S. dollar.
The rate was mainly used to calculate oil revenues. Syria produces around 600,000 barrels per day of crude oil and exports about 320,000.
Officials said several exchange rates were still used in the budget, although the main rate was the "encouragement rate" of 43.5 pounds to a dollar.
The 1996 budget was mainly based on the "encouragement rate" of 42 pounds to a dollar. The rate on the black market currently ranges between 50 and 52 pounds to a dollar.
The Syrian finance minister said the government would continue trying to unify the exchange rate against hard currencies but did not set a deadline.
Officials quoted Economy and Foreign Trade Minister Mohammed Imadi as saying in a separate meeting that the 1998 budget would be based on one rate.
"The government will continue its efforts to gradually unify the pound's rate and continue at the same time its efforts to keep stability in the pound's value," Mahayni said.

The minister said investment in 1997, 51.5 per cent of the total budget, was the largest share ever in a Syrian budget. He said the money would go to projects in the agricultural, industrial, electricity and communications sectors.
Investment spending in the 1996 budget stood at 91.5 billion pounds while current expenditure was 96.58 billion pounds.
